The feeder identifier is a numeric code that, when combined with grid topology data, can identify a specific geographic area and the consumers within it. This constitutes identifying information that could be used to narrow down to specific households or businesses, violating the principle of data minimization and purpose limitation under GDPR. Anonymization through generalization or pseudonymization is recommended.

The substation identifier, like the feeder, is a numeric code that can be mapped to a specific geographic location in the power grid. When combined with other data in the dataset, it enables re-identification of specific areas and potentially individual consumers. This is identifying data that should be anonymized to prevent location-based re-identification.

The date column contains temporal information that, on its own, does not constitute personal data. While dates can be part of a re-identification attack when combined with other quasi-identifiers, in this aggregate infrastructure dataset with 70+ housing units, the temporal dimension alone does not enable identification of specific individuals. The data is already at an aggregate level.

The housing units count (70-72) is a small aggregate number that, when combined with the feeder and substation identifiers, can help identify a specific residential area. In small communities or specific neighborhoods, knowing the exact number of housing units can serve as a quasi-identifier. Under the principle of data minimization, this should be generalized (e.g., rounded to nearest 10) to prevent area-level re-identification.

The industry and commerce count (11) is a small number that, combined with the specific consumption categories (shop/hairdresser, bakery), can potentially identify specific businesses in the area. With only 11 commercial units, the combination of count and consumption type could narrow down to identifiable individual businesses, which constitutes personal data for sole proprietors or small business owners under GDPR.
